name: Demonstrative with an Oblique Genitive

1.definition: Picks out a referent through a demonstrative and a genitive relation, including a uniquely possessed referent.
1.details: Barker analyzes a demonstrative construction in which that nose of his is usable for an ordinary person with one nose, though the nose of his is degraded. He links the use to focus on the head and speaker affect. The extent to which affect is required across CGEL’s examples remains open.

examples.note: The phrase can be tested in a setting with a single husband.
Plural demonstrative in CGEL's oblique-genitive series.
Published judgment in comparison with the nose of his.

relatedConstructions.notes: The demonstrative marks the NP as definite.
The of-phrase takes an independent genitive NP.

grounds.note: Distinguishes the demonstrative pattern from oblique genitives subject to anti-uniqueness.

projection.target: The demonstrative form can license an oblique genitive even when the relation supplies only one relevant referent.
projection.evidence: Barker's controlled contrast and the range of relations in CGEL's demonstrative series.

curious.title: That husband of Mary's
curious.summary: A demonstrative plus a phrase like of Mary's can pick out a person or thing through a relation, even when only one fits.
curious.body: In that husband of Mary's, the word that points to the husband, and the phrase of Mary's says whose husband he is. The same pattern appears in those green eyes of Mary's and that nose of his. The pattern works even when there is only one husband, or one nose, in the picture. This dictionary links this use to focus on the head noun and to speaker feeling, but how far feeling is needed across all the examples remains open. This dictionary treats the analysis as provisional.
curious.try: Compare that nose of his with his nose. Does the first one feel different?

teacher.summary: Helps explain that husband of Mary's and similar phrases with a demonstrative and an of-phrase containing a genitive.
teacher.explain: The pattern is NP[demonstrative determiner + nominal with an of-phrase containing a genitive NP]. The demonstrative marks the NP as definite, and the genitive relation picks out a referent, including a uniquely possessed one: that husband of Mary's can be tested in a setting with a single husband. A published analysis (Barker, 1998) distinguishes this demonstrative pattern from oblique genitives subject to anti-uniqueness, and links the use to focus on the head and speaker affect. How far affect is required across CGEL's examples remains open. The analysis is provisional.
teacher.terms: The of-phrase contains an independent genitive (Mary's, his), This grammar says genitive rather than possessive.

contrasts.note: Demonstrative with an oblique genitive; usable where Mary has one husband.
Plain genitive in determiner function; no demonstrative.

watch_for: A learner might think that husband of Mary's must mean Mary has several husbands, when the pattern can be used with a single one.
A learner might treat the demonstrative as only a pointing word, when the use is linked to focus and speaker affect.
teacher.activity: Give students pairs such as that husband of Mary's and Mary's husband. They say in which setting each would be natural and discuss whether the demonstrative version carries extra feeling.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Demonstrative with an Oblique Genitive." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/demonstrative-oblique-genitive-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, ef810bb).
